strong.text: Strong run. You read routes, qualifiers and patient context rather than reciting keys, and your answers held under the traps. Use the review cards to keep it sharp rather than to repair anything.

mixed.text: A mixed result. Some of the hernia anatomy and management logic is firm, and some still rests on recall. The sections below show which, and the review order starts with the weakest.

weak.text: Several core areas need rebuilding. That is useful information, not a verdict. Start with the first review cards listed below, and retake the journey after a day.

secure.text: Direct versus indirect is solid: you decide from the route relative to the inferior epigastric vessels, not from the names.

shaky.text: Direct versus indirect is partly there. Anchor one rule: indirect is lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels through the deep ring, direct is medial through the posterior wall.

gap.text: Direct versus indirect is a gap. Rebuild it from the route: the indirect sac enters at the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels; the direct sac bulges through the posterior wall, medial to them.

secure.text: Hesselbach's triangle is secure: three sides, the inguinal ligament as the exam-key base, and no rings.

shaky.text: Hesselbach's triangle is shaky. Say the three sides aloud: inferior epigastric artery, lateral rectus border, inguinal ligament. Exam keys use the inguinal ligament, not Cooper's, as the base.

gap.text: Hesselbach's triangle is a gap. Rebuild it from the inferior epigastric artery, lateral rectus border and inguinal ligament. Rings and the conjoint tendon are neighbours, not sides.

secure.text: Telling inguinal from femoral by the pubic tubercle is secure.

shaky.text: Inguinal versus femoral position is shaky. Fix it: inguinal is above and medial to the pubic tubercle, femoral is below and lateral.

gap.text: Inguinal versus femoral position is a gap. Femoral lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, inguinal above and medial. Trace the femoral canal below the inguinal ligament.

secure.text: Cause and clinical picture are secure: indirect congenital and often scrotal, direct acquired and rarely scrotal.

shaky.text: Cause and clinical picture are shaky. Pair them: indirect with patent processus, scrotal descent and lateral reduction; direct with acquired wall weakness and straight-back reduction.

gap.text: Cause and clinical picture are a gap. Indirect is congenital, from a patent processus vaginalis, and follows the cord into the scrotum. Direct is acquired, from posterior wall weakness, and rarely reaches the scrotum.

secure.text: The occlusion test and Zieman's test are secure: you map each result to the sac it separates.

shaky.text: The bedside tests are shaky. Predict each from anatomy: occlusion controls an indirect sac, and Zieman's index, middle and ring fingers sit over the deep ring, superficial ring and saphenous opening.

gap.text: The bedside tests are a gap. Occlusion of the deep ring controls an indirect sac while a direct sac still appears medial. In Zieman's test, index suggests indirect, middle direct, ring finger femoral.

secure.text: The 'most common' answers are secure, including the trap that femoral is only relatively commoner in women.

shaky.text: The 'most common' answers are shaky. Remember that indirect inguinal leads overall, in both sexes and in children, even though femoral is relatively commoner in women.

gap.text: The 'most common' answers are a gap. Indirect inguinal hernia is the commonest type overall, in both sexes and in children. Femoral is only relatively commoner in women, and a left sliding hernia most often contains sigmoid colon.

secure.text: Strangulation risk is secure: indirect beats direct for inguinal hernias, and femoral beats both when the stem says groin.

shaky.text: Strangulation risk is shaky. Two rankings: among inguinal hernias indirect strangulates more than direct, but among all groin hernias femoral is highest. Read the scope word.

gap.text: Strangulation risk is a gap. Indirect strangulates more than direct because of its narrow neck, and femoral is the highest-risk groin hernia. The scope word, inguinal or groin, decides which ranking applies.

secure.text: First step and investigation are secure: resuscitate and operate when strangulation is suspected, and match imaging to the question.

shaky.text: First step and investigation are shaky. Strangulation signs mean resuscitation and emergency surgery with no forceful taxis. For tests: none if evident, ultrasound for occult, MRI if inconclusive.

gap.text: First step and investigation are a gap. A strangulated hernia needs resuscitation and emergency surgery, never forceful taxis. An evident hernia needs no imaging; an occult one needs ultrasound first, then MRI if inconclusive.

secure.text: Choosing the operation is secure: you match it to the patient, not to what is newest or oldest.

shaky.text: Choosing the operation is shaky. Sort by patient: child herniotomy, adult open Lichtenstein, bilateral or recurrent laparoscopic, Shouldice as the best tissue repair. Older keys said Bassini.

gap.text: Choosing the operation is a gap. Child: herniotomy alone. Adult open: Lichtenstein mesh repair, with older keys saying Bassini. Bilateral or recurrent after open: laparoscopic TEP or TAPP. Best tissue repair: Shouldice.

secure.text: Nerves and triangles are secure: ilioinguinal in open, lateral femoral cutaneous in laparoscopic, doom vascular, pain neural.

shaky.text: Nerves and triangles are shaky. Pair them: ilioinguinal with open repair, lateral femoral cutaneous with laparoscopic repair, doom with vessels, pain with nerves.

gap.text: Nerves and triangles are a gap. Ilioinguinal is the nerve most injured in open repair; lateral femoral cutaneous in laparoscopic. The triangle of doom holds the external iliac vessels, the triangle of pain holds nerves.

secure.text: The named hernias are secure: you anchor each eponym to its contents and site.

shaky.text: The named hernias are shaky. Anchor each: Amyand is appendix in an inguinal sac, de Garengeot appendix in a femoral sac, Littre has a Meckel's diverticulum, Richter traps part of the wall.

gap.text: The named hernias are a gap. Amyand is the appendix in an inguinal sac, de Garengeot the appendix in a femoral sac, Littre a Meckel's diverticulum, Richter part of the bowel wall, Maydl a W loop.

Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

The direct sac pushes through the posterior wall, medial to them. You may have fixed it on the spot, but that does not show it holds. Meet it again on a fresh question: do its review card next.

avoided.text: You held 'relatively more common in women' apart from 'most common in women'.

fell_recovered.text: You first read femoral hernia as the commonest in women, then separated a relative skew from a ranking: indirect inguinal still leads. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

fell_open.text: You read 'relatively more common in women' as 'most common in women', so a female skew overrode the ranking. Femoral hernia is relatively commoner in women than in men, but indirect inguinal hernia is still the most common hernia in women. Watch the word 'relatively' in superlative stems. You may have fixed it on the spot, but that does not show it holds. Meet it again on a fresh question: do its review card next.

avoided.text: You matched the operation to the child's defect: herniotomy for a patent processus.

fell_recovered.text: You started with an adult repair for a child, then tied the operation to the defect: a patent processus vaginalis with a normal posterior wall, so herniotomy alone. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

fell_open.text: You treated the child as a small adult and carried over the posterior wall repair or mesh. A child's defect is a patent processus vaginalis with a normal posterior wall, so herniotomy alone is the operation. Ask what the defect is before choosing the operation. You may have fixed it on the spot, but that does not show it holds. Meet it again on a fresh question: do its review card next.

avoided.text: You tied strangulation risk to the narrow neck, not the bulk of the swelling.

fell_recovered.text: You first judged strangulation risk by size, then reasoned from the neck: the narrow neck at the deep ring grips the contents. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

fell_open.text: You judged danger by the size of the swelling. Risk follows the neck: the indirect hernia's narrow neck at the deep ring strangulates more readily than the direct hernia's wide, diffuse bulge. Trace the neck first, then rank the two. You may have fixed it on the spot, but that does not show it holds. Meet it again on a fresh question: do its review card next.

avoided.text: You noticed that 'groin' widens the set to include femoral, which strangulates most.

fell_recovered.text: You first answered with the inguinal ranking, then read the scope word: 'groin' includes femoral, which has the highest strangulation risk. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

fell_open.text: You answered the narrower inguinal ranking when the stem said 'groin'. Among all groin hernias, femoral has the highest risk of strangulation; indirect only wins when the stem says inguinal. Underline the scope word in every superlative stem. You may have fixed it on the spot, but that does not show it holds. Meet it again on a fresh question: do its review card next.

avoided.text: You put resuscitation and emergency surgery before reduction in a strangulated hernia.

fell_recovered.text: You reached for manual reduction first, then ordered the steps around bowel viability: resuscitate, then emergency surgery, no forceful taxis. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

fell_open.text: You carried the reducible-hernia habit of pushing it back into a case where the bowel may be dead. Forceful taxis can push gangrenous bowel back or cause reduction en masse. With a tense, tender, toxic presentation, the first step is resuscitation and emergency surgery. You may have fixed it on the spot, but that does not show it holds. Meet it again on a fresh question: do its review card next.

avoided.text: You matched each test to the clinical question.

fell_recovered.text: You first chose the most advanced test, then used the ladder: no imaging for an evident hernia, ultrasound first for an occult one, MRI if ultrasound is inconclusive, CT for complications. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

fell_open.text: You picked tests by sophistication. A clinically evident hernia needs no imaging. Ultrasound is the first test for an occult hernia, MRI the step after an inconclusive ultrasound, and CT is kept for complicated or obscure cases. Ask evident, occult or complicated before choosing. You may have fixed it on the spot, but that does not show it holds. Meet it again on a fresh question: do its review card next.

avoided.text: You kept the nerve tied to the approach: ilioinguinal in open, lateral femoral cutaneous in laparoscopic.

fell_recovered.text: You first applied one nerve to both approaches, then tied each to its field: ilioinguinal in open repair, lateral femoral cutaneous in laparoscopic repair. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

fell_open.text: You reused one famous nerve for both approaches without reading the setting word. Ilioinguinal is the nerve most often injured in open repair; the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is most at risk in laparoscopic repair, giving anterolateral thigh paraesthesia. Pair each nerve with its field of dissection. You may have fixed it on the spot, but that does not show it holds. Meet it again on a fresh question: do its review card next.

avoided.text: You read the qualifiers before choosing open or laparoscopic.

fell_recovered.text: You first picked laparoscopic by default, then used the qualifiers: bilateral or recurrent favours it, and it needs general anaesthesia and expertise. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

fell_open.text: You treated 'newer' as 'default' and chose laparoscopic repair without reading the qualifiers. Bilateral hernia and recurrence after open repair favour it; laparoscopic repair needs general anaesthesia and a learning curve, so a primary unilateral hernia without expertise stays open. Check the qualifiers first. You may have fixed it on the spot, but that does not show it holds. Meet it again on a fresh question: do its review card next.

avoided.text: You answered with current practice and knew the older key.

fell_recovered.text: You started with the older Bassini key, then learned both: older PYQs expected Bassini, current practice is Lichtenstein mesh repair. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

fell_open.text: You answered from the older textbook key. Older PYQs expected Bassini, but the standard open repair now is Lichtenstein tension-free mesh repair, with Shouldice as the best tissue repair. Learn both keys, and read the stem for which era it wants. You may have fixed it on the spot, but that does not show it holds. Meet it again on a fresh question: do its review card next.

avoided.text: You predicted the deep ring occlusion test from where each sac comes through.

fell_recovered.text: You first reversed the occlusion test, then worked out which sac the finger blocks: an indirect sac is controlled, a direct sac still bulges medial to the finger. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

fell_open.text: You memorised the occlusion test result without its mechanism, so it flipped. Pressure over the deep ring blocks the route of an indirect sac, which stays controlled on coughing; a direct sac comes through the posterior wall and still appears medial to the finger. Predict the sac's exit before choosing. You may have fixed it on the spot, but that does not show it holds. Meet it again on a fresh question: do its review card next.

avoided.text: You mapped each finger or fingertip to the ring or depth it covers.

fell_recovered.text: You swapped the finger sites, then tied each to its anatomy: index over the deep ring, middle over the superficial ring, ring finger over the saphenous opening. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

fell_open.text: You recalled fingertip rules by rote order rather than by anatomy. In Zieman's test the index finger sits over the deep ring (indirect), middle over the superficial ring (direct), ring finger over the saphenous opening (femoral). In the invagination test the tip suggests indirect and the pulp direct. You may have fixed it on the spot, but that does not show it holds. Meet it again on a fresh question: do its review card next.

avoided.text: You kept the clinical pictures of the two inguinal hernias apart.

fell_recovered.text: You first gave the scrotal swelling to the direct hernia, then compared them side by side: the indirect sac follows the cord into the scrotum. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

fell_open.text: You attached the scrotal swelling to the direct hernia, the one that sounds more severe. The indirect sac follows the cord down the canal: pear-shaped, often reaching the scrotum, reducing up, lateral and back. The direct hernia is globular, near the pubic tubercle, reduces straight back and rarely reaches the scrotum. You may have fixed it on the spot, but that does not show it holds. Meet it again on a fresh question: do its review card next.

avoided.text: You kept the triangle of doom vascular and the triangle of pain neural.

fell_recovered.text: You swapped the two triangles, then separated them: doom holds the external iliac vessels, pain holds the nerves, with the gonadal vessels as the divider. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

fell_open.text: You filed both triangles as 'no-tack zones' and swapped their contents. Doom lies between the vas deferens and gonadal vessels and holds the external iliac vessels. Pain lies lateral to the gonadal vessels, below the iliopubic tract, and holds the lateral femoral cutaneous, genitofemoral branch and femoral nerves. You may have fixed it on the spot, but that does not show it holds. Meet it again on a fresh question: do its review card next.

avoided.text: You put the conjoint tendon on the posterior wall, where it belongs.

fell_recovered.text: You first put the conjoint tendon in the anterior wall, then compared the walls: the anterior wall is external oblique with internal oblique laterally; the posterior wall is transversalis fascia with the conjoint tendon medially. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

fell_open.text: You placed the conjoint tendon beside internal oblique, so on the anterior wall. The anterior wall is external oblique aponeurosis, reinforced laterally by internal oblique. The posterior wall is transversalis fascia, reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon. Place structures by the wall they reinforce. You may have fixed it on the spot, but that does not show it holds. Meet it again on a fresh question: do its review card next.

avoided.text: You paired each hernia with its cause: indirect congenital, direct acquired.

fell_recovered.text: You first gave direct hernia a congenital cause, then paired each with its own: indirect arises in a patent processus vaginalis, direct from posterior wall weakness. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

fell_open.text: You assumed direct and indirect differ only in position, so you swapped their causes. Indirect hernia is congenital, from a patent processus vaginalis; direct is acquired, from posterior wall weakness. Complete persistence of the processus gives a congenital hernia reaching the testis, partial gives a funicular hernia. You may have fixed it on the spot, but that does not show it holds. Meet it again on a fresh question: do its review card next.

avoided.text: You anchored the appendix hernias to their sites.

fell_recovered.text: You swapped Amyand and de Garengeot, then anchored each to its site: Amyand inguinal, de Garengeot femoral. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

fell_open.text: You knew both eponyms hold the appendix but not which site goes with which. Amyand's hernia is the appendix in an inguinal sac; de Garengeot is the appendix in a femoral sac. Learn each with its site, and contrast Littre (Meckel's), Richter (part of the wall) and Maydl (W loop). You may have fixed it on the spot, but that does not show it holds. Meet it again on a fresh question: do its review card next.

avoided.text: You separated sac excision, own-tissue repair and mesh repair.

fell_recovered.text: You mixed the three operation terms, then ordered them by what is added to sac excision: herniotomy none, herniorrhaphy own tissue, hernioplasty mesh. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

fell_open.text: You treated the three operation terms as interchangeable. Herniotomy is sac excision alone. Herniorrhaphy adds repair of the posterior wall with the patient's own tissue. Hernioplasty reinforces the wall with prosthetic mesh, so a mesh repair is not herniorrhaphy. You may have fixed it on the spot, but that does not show it holds. Meet it again on a fresh question: do its review card next.

avoided.text: You placed the femoral hernia below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.

fell_recovered.text: You first copied the inguinal position onto the femoral hernia, then traced its route below the inguinal ligament. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

fell_open.text: You gave the femoral hernia the inguinal position. An inguinal hernia emerges above and medial to the pubic tubercle; a femoral hernia lies below and lateral. Anchor the femoral neck below the inguinal ligament, and the position will stop being copied across. You may have fixed it on the spot, but that does not show it holds. Meet it again on a fresh question: do its review card next.

E1.text: You tend to mix up look-alike pairs, such as direct versus indirect pictures or the three operation terms. Next time, name the one feature that separates them before choosing.

E2.text: You tend to add familiar neighbours to a fixed set. Rebuild a set from its logic and ask which option is not a member.

E3.text: You tend to get a direction backwards, such as lateral versus medial, or what a test blocks. Predict the route first, then pick the answer.

E4.text: You tend to stretch 'relatively more' into 'most'. Check qualifiers on superlatives before answering.

E5.text: You tend to answer from an older key when practice has moved on. Ask whether the stem wants the old PYQ key or current practice.

E7.text: You tend to skip qualifiers such as child versus adult, groin versus inguinal, open versus laparoscopic. Underline the qualifier before reading the options.

E8.text: You tend to pick tests by sophistication. Match the test to the question: none, ultrasound, MRI, then CT for complications.

E9.text: You tend to do the right things in the wrong order. Ask what must come first and why; here, bowel viability comes before reduction.

E10.text: You tend to mismatch eponyms and associations: fingers, causes, triangles or appendix hernias. Practise them as paired recall with the discriminating feature.

overconfident.text: You tapped Sure on more than one answer that turned out wrong. Those are the errors that survive revision, so review them first and treat a Sure tap as a prompt to check the qualifier.

underconfident.text: You tapped Guessing on several answers that were right. Your reasoning is better than you credit; when you can state the route or the rule, tap Sure.

calibrated.text: Your confidence tracked your accuracy: Sure where you were right, more cautious where you were not. Keep that habit in the exam.

hints_heavy.text: You opened many hints. Using them is fine, but try the next review card cold, answering before looking, so the report can show what you recall unaided.

hints_none.text: You used no hints, so the traps you fell into were honest misses. Next time, a hint after a doubt is cheaper than a wrong first answer.

hinted_only.text: Some objectives were right only after a hint. Retry those review cards without hints; unaided recall is what the exam tests.

fast_lane.text: You earned the fast lane by answering the diagnostic correctly and sure. The review cards will tell you whether that holds a week from now.

gap.text: Do the review cards in the order listed: confident errors first, then gaps, then shaky areas. Retry the journey after a day, and tackle one gap per sitting.

clear.text: No gaps. Run the review cards on their schedule so the anatomy rules, scope words and operation choices stay available under exam pressure.
